metadata.description: Telecom civil construction in Green Bay, WI — deep-frost foundations, duct bank, and compound work for fiber, wireless, and edge builds across Brown County.
metadata.h1: Telecom Site Civil Construction in Green Bay, Wisconsin
metadata.intro: Green Bay sits at the cold end of our footprint, and the civil work here shows it: footings driven at least 48 inches down under Wisconsin's frost rules, a construction calendar bracketed by frozen-road declarations and Class II spring thaw restrictions, and red lacustrine clays in the eastern valleys that behave nothing like upland till. CellSite Solutions serves the Green Bay market from our Cedar Rapids yard — 304 road miles down the US-151/I-41 corridor — self-performing shelter and hut foundations, underground and duct bank, grounding, and compound construction across Brown County, with Wisconsin's own wetland permitting and Diggers Hotline timelines built into every schedule.

geotech.dominantGeology: Brown County's bedrock is an eastward-dipping Cambrian–Ordovician–Silurian sequence of sandstone, dolostone, and shale, with the Silurian dolostone forming the Niagara Escarpment cuesta through the eastern county. Above it lie Pleistocene glacial and proglacial sediments up to roughly 330 feet thick — with red lacustrine clays prevalent in the eastern valleys, locally 250–300 feet thick, interstratified with sand and gravel — and buried bedrock valleys under the glacial fill. (WGNHS Brown County bedrock mapping; USGS artesian aquifer studies.)
dominantSoilTypes: Kewaunee silty clay loam (dominant series, ~89,700 acres)
Superior red clays and clay loams

karstRisk.note: Verified karst — enlarged joints and sinkholes — occurs in the Silurian dolomite along the Niagara Escarpment in eastern Brown County, and the dolomite aquifer is documented as highly susceptible to contamination (WGNHS; USGS). Escarpment-side sites warrant karst screening in the geotech scope.

geotech.foundationApproachNarrative: Two things set foundations apart in Green Bay: depth and clay. Wisconsin's frost rule puts footings at least 48 inches below adjacent grade — deeper than anywhere else in our footprint — so every shelter pier, hut footing, and bollard carries real excavation even before loads enter the conversation, and winter work means frost ripping through the top of that column. The second variable is the red lacustrine clay of the eastern valleys: fine-grained, moisture-sensitive, and slow-draining, it punishes open excavations in wet season and rewards careful subgrade protection. On the eastern side of the county, the Niagara Escarpment brings shallow dolostone and documented karst into play — pier sockets get attractive, but voids get screened first. Site-specific geotechnical investigation governs; the borings decide which of these three stories your site is telling.

regulatory.permitTimelineNarrative: Commercial building work in Green Bay runs under the state's uniform code (SPS 361–366, now on the 2021 IBC) with the city's Building Inspection Division as the local AHJ; larger projects add state plan review. The two timeline items that catch out-of-state schedulers are Wisconsin-specific: Diggers Hotline wants three business days' notice before excavation, and the WDNR construction stormwater NOI must be in at least 14 working days before land disturbance — roughly three weeks of lead on any compound or route disturbing an acre. Wetland involvement adds WDNR permitting even where the federal 404 program wouldn't reach, because Wisconsin regulates nonfederal wetlands under Wis. Stat. 281.36.

seasonality.narrative: Green Bay's construction year is the shortest in our footprint and the most rule-bound. Deep frost holds the ground from roughly December into April, and the road network follows its own sequence — frozen-road declarations in winter, then Class II spring thaw restrictions on state highways (2026: February 20 through April 30) with county and town postings layered on top. The productive window is effectively May through October, front-loaded against June's peak rainfall on slow-draining red clays and back-checked by the April–October bat-habitat clearing restriction. Winter work is done here, but it is planned work: frost ripping, heated enclosures, and hauls timed to the declarations. Confirm the calendar against the NCEI normals table for Austin Straubel International before final publication.

costDrivers.rockNote: Shallow Silurian dolostone along the Niagara Escarpment side of the county brings rock excavation — and karst screening — into eastern Brown County sites; the deep glacial valleys west of the escarpment rarely see rock at telecom depths.
costDrivers.spoilDisposalNote: Wet red lacustrine clay spoil is heavy, slow to dry, and unattractive as fill — plan disposal and import balance accordingly on eastern-valley sites.
costDrivers.prevailingWageExposure: Wisconsin repealed its state prevailing wage laws (2017 Act 59; state projects bid after Sept 23, 2017, local after Jan 1, 2018). Federal Davis-Bacon still applies to federally funded work — including BEAD-funded broadband builds.
costDrivers.seasonalPremiumNote: The deepest seasonal premium in our footprint: 48-inch footings through frost, winter concrete protection December through March, and spring-restriction routing for any heavy haul from roughly late February to early May.
costDrivers.narrative: Green Bay's cost drivers are the calendar and the clay. Every foundation buys 48 inches of depth before loads are considered, and buying it in winter adds frost excavation and heated cures. Spring adds routing cost instead: Class II restrictions and locally posted roads can turn a 30-minute shelter haul into a staged delivery. The eastern county's red clays drive dewatering, subgrade protection, and spoil handling, while escarpment-side sites trade clay problems for rock and karst screening. Wisconsin's broad wetland jurisdiction — nonfederal wetlands included — adds permitting scope other states don't have, with a 14-working-day stormwater NOI lead on top. Mobilization from Cedar Rapids is a scheduled overnight-crew item rather than a premium. Drivers, never unit prices; each site prices to its borings and its month.

compliance.stateContractorLicensing: Wisconsin issues no statewide license for commercial general contractors — commercial work is governed through permits, plan review, and trade-specific credentials, and the DSPS Dwelling Contractor certification applies only to 1–2 family residential work. Electrical and plumbing trades carry their own state credentials. Verify current requirements against DSPS directly, as this summary was compiled from secondary sources.

hazards.designImplications: Cold is the design driver: a −12°F heating design temperature, 48-inch frost embedment, and roughly 55 inches of annual snow shape foundations, HVAC sizing, and generator enclosures. Ice loading on structures should be published only after Brown County TIA-222 values are confirmed. Along the Fox River and bay shoreline, the floodplain overlay adds elevation and permitting requirements.

items.headline: Wisconsin BEAD final proposal approved — $1.06B, 76% fiber
items.detail: NTIA approved Wisconsin's final BEAD proposal (allocation $1,055,823,573) in December 2025, administered by the PSC of Wisconsin, with an award mix of roughly 76% fiber, 10% fixed wireless, and 14% satellite plus $397M in matching funds — a statewide rural fiber construction pipeline.

items.headline: Microsoft Mount Pleasant campus keeps expanding
items.detail: Microsoft completed its AI supercomputer data center at Mount Pleasant (Racine County) in June 2026, announced a $4B second facility in September 2025, and holds approval for 15 more buildings — the state's largest construction program, about 130 miles south of Green Bay.

items.headline: Vantage 'Lighthouse' campus underway at Port Washington
items.detail: The Vantage/Cloverleaf hyperscale campus in Port Washington (Ozaukee County) broke ground in December 2025 — four buildings, ~2.5M sq ft, up to 902 MW, completion targeted 2028 — reinforcing eastern Wisconsin's I-41/I-43 corridor as a digital infrastructure geography.

fiber.narrative: Wisconsin's BEAD program — approved in December 2025 at $1.06B with roughly three-quarters of awards going to fiber — puts sustained rural fiber construction into the counties around Green Bay. The build conditions are distinctly Wisconsin: Diggers Hotline wants three business days before any excavation, the WDNR stormwater NOI needs 14 working days, and the state's wetland jurisdiction reaches nonfederal wetlands that a 404-only mindset would miss. Physically, boring the eastern valleys means slow-draining red lacustrine clay, while escarpment-side routes meet shallow dolomite. FOXY's shortline out of Green Bay toward Luxemburg and Denmark is the crossing most likely to sit over a Brown County route. Hut foundations go 48 inches down like everything else here.

secondaryScopeIds: small cell and DAS node civil
wireless.narrative: Wireless civil in Green Bay is scheduled around frost twice over. Foundations go at least 48 inches below grade under Wisconsin's rule — the deepest requirement in our footprint — and the road network runs its own frost calendar: heavy shelter hauls ride the winter frozen-road declarations or wait out Class II spring restrictions, which ran February 20 through April 30 in 2026, with locally posted county roads the usual binding constraint. Tree clearing in suitable northern long-eared bat habitat is confined outside the April–October restriction with roost trees protected midsummer, which pushes greenfield clearing into winter. Small-cell work follows the statewide Act 14 framework with its $250-per-node annual cap. We build all of it with crews that treat −12°F design weather as a plannable condition, not an emergency.

edge.narrative: Green Bay has no announced hyperscale campus of its own — the honest picture is that Wisconsin's data center gravity sits 130 miles south, where Microsoft's Mount Pleasant program keeps expanding and the Vantage Port Washington campus broke ground in late 2025. What that buildout does for Green Bay is pull the I-41/I-43 corridor into the state's digital infrastructure map: edge enclosures, carrier micro-sites, and utility-yard work follow fiber and power capacity north. WPS — headquartered in Green Bay and serving 474,000 electric customers across the northeast — is the interconnection counterparty for new load here. Edge pads in this climate carry the same 48-inch embedment, snow-shedding, and generator cold-weather packages as any northern compound, which is exactly the work our crews standardize.

operations.mobilizationNote: Green Bay sits 304 road miles from our Cedar Rapids yard — up US-151 through Dubuque and Madison, then I-41 north through the Fox Valley — a run our crews treat as an overnight-stay market rather than a day trip: mobilize once, work the week, demobilize once. The route itself has seasonal texture that we plan around rather than discover: Class II spring restrictions on Wisconsin highways and locally posted county roads shape when heavy loads and equipment moves happen (2026: late February through the end of April), and winter runs on the I-41 corridor get weather windows built in. Multi-site programs across Brown County and the Fox Valley batch efficiently from a single mobilization. Response commitments beyond that are stated only after ops sign-off.

faq.question: How deep do telecom foundations need to go in Green Bay?
faq.answer: At least 48 inches below adjacent grade — Wisconsin's frost rule (SPS 321.16 puts footings below frost penetration or 48 inches, whichever is deeper) is the deepest requirement in our nine-state footprint. Every shelter pier, hut footing, and fence post foundation carries that excavation, and winter installs add frost ripping above it. Confirm the commercial-code application with the city's Building Inspection Division for your specific project.

faq.question: Do spring road restrictions affect shelter delivery to Green Bay sites?
faq.answer: Decisively. Wisconsin posts Class II spring thaw restrictions on about 1,400 miles of state highways — in 2026 they ran February 20 through April 30 — and county and town roads post their own limits, which are usually the binding constraint for the last miles to a rural compound. We schedule heavy sets either on winter frozen-road declarations or after the postings lift, and route around posted segments in between.

faq.question: How much notice does Diggers Hotline require before excavation?
faq.answer: Three business days under Wis. Stat. 182.0175 — a day longer than the Texas and Iowa one-call centers in our footprint. We file tickets as soon as a dig date firms up, and pair that lead with the WDNR stormwater NOI clock (14 working days before disturbance on 1-acre-plus sites) so neither wait lands on the critical path twice.

faq.question: What's different about wetland permitting on Wisconsin fiber routes?
faq.answer: Wisconsin regulates nonfederal wetlands, not just federal ones. Under Wis. Stat. 281.36, filling any wetland needs a WDNR general or individual permit — the DNR permit also serves as the federal water quality certification — with only narrow exemptions (up to 1 acre urban / 3 acres rural, with 15-day pre-notification). Routes planned on a 404-only assumption get surprised here; we screen alignments against wetland mapping before locking them.

faq.question: Can you pour a shelter pad in Green Bay in January?
faq.answer: Yes — it's planned winter work. January normals run 25.5°F highs and 11.1°F lows with the season's heaviest snow, so pours get heated enclosures or blankets, warm mix, and cure monitoring, and excavation rips through established frost. The offsetting advantage: frozen-road declarations can actually make winter the easier season to move heavy loads on some routes.

faq.question: What tree-clearing restrictions apply on Brown County sites?
faq.answer: The northern long-eared bat sets the calendar. Under WisDOT's guidance, clearing in suitable habitat is restricted April 1 through October 31, occupied maternity roost trees (and trees within 150 feet) are protected June 1 – July 31, and nothing comes down within a quarter mile of a hibernaculum. Practically, greenfield clearing gets planned for winter. A project-specific IPaC query confirms what applies to your parcel.

faq.question: Who serves electric power for a new hut or compound in Green Bay?
faq.answer: Wisconsin Public Service — headquartered in Green Bay and part of WEC Energy Group — serves roughly 474,000 electric customers across northeast Wisconsin. New commercial service timelines aren't published, so we get the utility's confirmation in writing during scoping rather than assuming a transformer date, and we design generator pads so sites can commission ahead of permanent power if the schedule demands it.

faq.question: What soil conditions should we expect boring near the bay?
faq.answer: Red lacustrine clay — fine-grained, moisture-sensitive, and locally 250 to 300 feet thick in the eastern valleys. It bores predictably when handled at the right moisture but makes wet-season open cuts and spoil handling slow. East of the city along the Niagara Escarpment the picture flips to shallow Silurian dolomite with documented karst, so escarpment-side routes get rock tooling and void screening instead. Borings tell you which route you're on.

decisionGuidance.heading: When frost depth and frost laws set your Green Bay schedule
decisionGuidance.body: Green Bay punishes schedules built from a generic Midwest template, because two frost clocks run here and they don't align. The ground clock says foundations go 48 inches down, ground is hard-frozen December into April, and concrete needs winter protection at both ends of the season. The road clock is offset from it: the state's frozen-road declaration actually makes midwinter the best window to move a 40,000-pound shelter on some routes, while the Class II spring restrictions — plus locally posted county roads — close the same routes exactly when the ground starts to open up. The planning consequence is concrete: if a spring in-service date is fixed, either set the shelter in late winter on the frozen-road window and build around it as the ground thaws, or accept that the haul waits for postings to lift in May and compress everything behind it. Layer the bat-clearing calendar (greenfield clearing effectively pushed to winter) and the WDNR 14-working-day stormwater lead on top, and the sequencing decision — not production rates — is what determines whether a Green Bay site makes its date. We plan these builds backward from the haul.
